li.a: International Commission of Jurists: ICJ condemns the bomb attack in Israel (23 January 1995)
United Nations, Question of Palestine: Attack in Beit Lid, letter from Israel
Time magazine: Interview with a fanatic (archived page)
Al Jazeera: Fathi Shaqaqi: Don't Kill Him in Damascus
The Yeshiva World: Beit Lid memorial dedication after 13 years

content.p: On Sunday 22 January 1995, two Palestinian men set off explosives minutes apart at a bus stop at the Beit Lid junction in central Israel. The first blast came among soldiers who had gathered there after the weekend. The second came as people ran to help. The attack killed soldiers and one civilian, by the count of the International Commission of Jurists, and wounded dozens more. Palestinian Islamic Jihad claimed it. The figures for the dead differ from one account to another, and each figure below is given with the party that stated it.

Al Jazeera's account of the day says two members of Islamic Jihad, an armed Palestinian group, disguised themselves as Israeli soldiers and went to a busy crossroads between Tel Aviv and Haifa. The Yeshiva World, which describes the scene at a hitchhiking post in the Sharon area, says the men mingled with the crowd. Its account is that the first bomber dropped to the ground as if he were ill, and that soldiers ran to help him before he set off the explosives he carried.

The times differ. Israel's letter to the United Nations gives about 9:20 in the morning. Al Jazeera and the Yeshiva World both give about 9:30. In all three accounts the second bomber came later, after rescuers had arrived. The Yeshiva World adds that a third device was found at the scene, and that a third bomber never reached the spot.
content.h2: Who was killed, and who counted what
content.p: The International Commission of Jurists issued a statement on 23 January 1995, the day after the attack. It said the bombing had killed 18 Israeli soldiers and one civilian and injured "tens of other persons." It called on the Israeli government to show maximum restraint and to avoid collective action against Palestinian civilians, who it said had not committed the attack.

Israel's letter to the UN Security Council and General Assembly gave a lower count of 19 people killed and 66 wounded, 13 of them in critical condition. The letter said rescuers who had come to help the victims of the first explosion themselves became victims when the second went off.

Al Jazeera's 2018 documentary said an estimated 21 Israeli soldiers died, and it counted the two bombers separately. The Yeshiva World, reporting on a later memorial, said 22 people were murdered and that 21 of them were soldiers. The figures differ on whether the bombers are included in the totals. Each count is the claim of the party that made it.
content.h2: The claim and the group's own account
content.p: Israel's letter to the UN said Islamic Jihad had claimed the attack and said it had been carried out by two of its members from the Gaza Strip. The letter also said thousands of Islamic Jihad supporters had gathered outside the homes of the two men in Gaza to celebrate the killings. The letter described the attackers' organisations as receiving support and guidance from certain states in the region, and said those organisations bore responsibility for the violence no less than the perpetrators themselves.

Four days after the bombing, Time magazine interviewed Fathi Shaqaqi, the group's founder, in Damascus. The magazine spelled his name Shkaki. He said the two men had gone to the site beforehand, and that he had known one of the bombers as a boy in Gaza. He said he did not choose the bombers himself, that the group's military branch did, and that he would not say whether he had known in advance. Asked whether the attack gave him satisfaction, he said: "It gives satisfaction to our people."

Shaqaqi also disclaimed direct responsibility. He told Time that it was "not logical to give orders or plan from outside," while admitting he had contacts with the movement. Al Jazeera's 2018 report says he plotted the attack from Damascus.
content.h2: The government response and the peace talks
content.p: The attack came in the middle of the peace process between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization. The Declaration of Principles had been signed on 13 September 1993. Israel's letter to the UN said 110 Israelis had been killed in 49 separate attacks by Palestinian militants in the period since then. The letter called on the international community to condemn the bombing and to refuse to let the militants decide the future of the region's peoples.

Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin went to Beit Lid to see the scene, according to Al Jazeera's interview with the Israeli journalist Ronen Bergman. Bergman described Rabin as having seen the bodies and as having faced protesters who wanted him to act. Al Jazeera also reported that Rabin allegedly ordered Shaqaqi killed immediately. That is an allegation, and the saved pages do not show an order.
content.h2: Damascus and the founder of Islamic Jihad
content.p: Al Jazeera describes Shaqaqi as a former Muslim Brotherhood member and maths teacher who studied medicine in Egypt. He founded Islamic Jihad in 1981, after growing frustrated with the Brotherhood's rejection of violence as a way to fight the occupation. Time reported that he was deported by Israel in 1988 and had been directing the group from a refugee camp in Damascus since 1989. Al Jazeera adds that he was later released from an Israeli prison early, and then moved to Syria as a guest of President Hafez al-Assad.
Al Jazeera says the group has claimed responsibility for more than 30 suicide bombings of military and civilian targets over the years. The report does not cite an official count.

Al Jazeera reports that Shaqaqi travelled to Malta on his way back from a visit to Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi. He checked into the Diplomat Hotel in the morning and was shot dead within five hours by two men on a motorcycle. Al Jazeera describes him as shot in the head five times at close range.

Bergman told Al Jazeera that the task of killing Shaqaqi fell to Kidon, a unit of Mossad, the Israeli intelligence service. Dr Anthony Abela Medici, a former director of the Malta Police's Forensic Science Laboratory, said the case had left open the possibility of a role for Libyan intelligence. "We cannot confirm which foreign side killed him," he said. Al Jazeera's report describes the Maltese investigators as reluctant to say who was responsible, so Mossad's role remains Bergman's claim rather than a finding.

The Yeshiva World reported that a memorial to the victims of the 1995 double suicide bombing was scheduled for dedication on a Tuesday, after thirteen years of efforts to finish it. Family members said they had campaigned for years for the memorial, and said government agencies had been slow to act. The monument shows a ladder rising towards heaven, with the victims climbing it.
